content: 1. Gender norms and roles must be addressed systematically within health programs to ensure inclusivity and equity. 2. All staff members should undergo comprehensive training to understand and address gender-related barriers in health interventions. 3. Training sessions should be scheduled at convenient times and locations, with accessible transport options to ensure participation by all staff. 4. Local health workers, including those addressing security and safety concerns, must be sensitized to gender-related issues. 5. Safe and reliable transportation must be provided for personnel, especially women, to ensure their safety and participation. 6. Collaboration with local women’s groups is essential to identify and implement practical solutions to gender-related challenges. 7. The composition of community-based surveillance (CBS) teams should be modified to ensure gender balance and inclusivity. 8. Delays in case investigation and stool collection can arise due to insufficient training opportunities for female surveillance officers, a lack of female officers to access homes of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) cases, and the inability of female caregivers to stay overnight in health facilities when cases are hospitalized. 9. Safety and security risks faced by female workers, such as mobility and transport challenges, must be addressed to ensure their effective participation. 10. Surveillance teams should be restructured to include a gender-balanced workforce, ensuring access to all households and communities. 11. Local health systems and communities must be sensitized to gender-related barriers and encouraged to support women’s participation in health programs. 12. Programs should systematically collect and analyze sex-disaggregated data to identify and address gender-related delays in detection, notification, and investigation of cases. 13. Surveillance officers and program managers should conduct in-depth assessments with the support of gender specialists to identify gaps and implement locally acceptable solutions. 14. Collaboration with women’s groups, grassroots networks, and organizations with expertise in health-seeking behaviors and gender barriers is critical to improving health outcomes. 15. Community authorities, religious leaders, and opinion influencers, including women, should be consulted to negotiate access to households and increase women’s participation in health programs. 16. Fathers and men should be encouraged to participate equally in childcare, caregiving, and household responsibilities to promote gender equality. 17. Communication materials and messages should be context-specific, informed by gender analysis, and free from harmful gender stereotypes. 18. Gender-related barriers to immunization and surveillance should be included in training and sensitization sessions conducted in health facilities or communities. 19. Equal parenting and shared caregiving responsibilities must be emphasized, with a focus on promoting fathers’ active involvement in childcare and household tasks. 20. Training visuals and materials should represent diverse women and men to ensure inclusivity. 21. The importance of collecting and analyzing sex-disaggregated data in all monitoring and evaluation activities must be highlighted. 22. Training sessions should be accessible to all participants, with safe and convenient facilities, appropriate timing, and inclusive seating arrangements. 23. Facilitators should be trained to ensure active participation from all attendees during training sessions. 24. Gender-related indicators, such as the proportion of AFP cases detected by sex and the timeliness of field activities, should be systematically monitored and reported. 25. All polio surveillance training must include a gender module, focusing on gender-related barriers in surveillance activities. 26. Regular provision of gender analysis in reports should be institutionalized to ensure ongoing evaluation and improvement. 27. Information on existing reporting and support mechanisms for addressing sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment must be shared with all staff. 28. Mandatory training on preventing and responding to sexual exploitation, abuse, and harassment should be conducted for all staff members. 29. Gender equality must be integrated into organizational policies and programming to create a safe and enabling work environment for all staff. 30. Gender-responsive communication strategies should be implemented to address barriers and promote equitable health outcomes. 31. Environmental sample collection for polio surveillance must follow standardized protocols, ensuring adequate sample volume, proper storage, and timely transportation to laboratories. 32. Observations during sample collection, such as wastewater characteristics or access issues, should be documented to improve surveillance accuracy. 33. The eligibility of children for antiviral polio treatment should be assessed, and appropriate follow-up stool testing should be conducted as required. 34. The number and type of polio vaccine doses received by children and their close family members should be recorded to monitor immunization coverage. 35. Guidelines and protocols for environmental surveillance and acute flaccid paralysis surveillance should be followed to ensure effective detection and response to polio cases. 36. Gender equality strategies and tools, such as the Gender Analysis Toolkit and Gender-Responsive Communication for Development, should be utilized to integrate gender considerations into health programs. 37. Efforts to eradicate polio must include gender-sensitive approaches to maximize the participation and safety of all stakeholders involved in surveillance and immunization activities.
